section_path_text: Pirates... What Arrr They Good For?
summary: Pirates on television can be charmingly swarthy, but there is nothing entertaining about the reality plaguing shipping markets off the Arabian Peninsula. In recent years, the rings of ship hijackers operating off the coast of East Africa have become more sophisticated and better organized, employing more aggressive tactics, and attacking merchant vessels more boldly and violently. The relatively slow speeds of fully laden tankers have made them vulnerable to hijacking attempts.

children.title: Suezmax (Reported)
children.summary: VLCC (Reported) Total Suez Canal Crossings ‐ 150‐300+kdwt While overall spot fixture activity out of the Arabian Gulf is expected to reach levels seen in 2008, the Suez Canal Authority has reported only 76 laden tankers larger than 150,000 dwt have transited the Suez Canal year to date, suggesting around 100 transits over the whole of 2011. This would reflect a decrease in activity of over 50% since 2008, when over 220 VLCC and Suezmax tankers were reported to have passed laden through the Canal on westbound voyages.

However, in a weak market, bunkers tend to account for a higher percentage of overall voyage costs, and the price of additional bunkers burned has more impact on owners' overall earnings.

children.title: Risky Business
children.summary: As piracy operations have become more sophisticated, deviation has ceased to be a fail‐safe protection against hijacking. Advancement in communications and the use of "motherships" have extended pirates' reach to areas further off the East African coast.

children.title: Keeping Close Guard
children.summary: The use of armed guards has been perhaps the most controversial anti‐piracy measure employed by the shipping industry. The Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO) estimated that armed guards are now present on 5‐10% of all transits through the Indian Ocean.
